data_centers.what: AI models run in giant warehouses of computers called data centers. Companies plan to spend trillions of dollars on them, and the biggest ones use as much electricity as a mid-sized city. Someone has to build the power plants and wires to feed them, and utilities usually spread those costs across everyone's bills.
data_centers.stakes: Household electricity prices jumped in 2025 and 2026, especially in the mid-Atlantic and Midwest grid regions, and data centers took much of the blame. Local fights over noise, water and land have flipped town councils in both red and blue areas. Supporters say the buildout is a national security race with China and a jobs boom; critics say families are subsidizing the richest companies on earth.
data_centers.recent: By September 2026 the fight had reached the House floor. The bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act (H.R. 9340), which pushes states to make data centers of 100 megawatts or more pay the full cost of the grid upgrades they trigger, cleared the Energy and Commerce Committee 52 to 0 and was scheduled for a vote the week of September 14. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez want a national moratorium on new AI data centers, and the committee's top Democrat, Frank Pallone, says a moratorium is on the table if guardrails fail. Some Republicans, including Sen. Tom Cotton and Chairman Brett Guthrie, have suggested China is stoking the backlash. The White House's voluntary Ratepayer Protection Pledge from March 2026 now has 187 corporate signers, and both parties are arguing over whether to write it into law.

labels.-2: Wants to pause new data centers or block projects until protections exist.
labels.-1: Data centers can be built, but only if families' bills, water and communities are protected first; mostly critical.
labels.0: Points both ways, or says the issue belongs to states and localities.
labels.1: Supports the buildout and says data centers should pay their own way.
labels.2: Wants faster permitting, federal land and fewer limits; treats the buildout as a race with China.

bills.label: H.R.9340
bills.title: Ratepayer Protection Act
bills.what: Adds a federal standard under PURPA that state utility regulators must consider: data-center customers of 100 MW or more must pay the full incremental cost of the generation, transmission and distribution upgrades built to serve them (even if they later leave), and post financial assurances up front. Aims to stop tech companies' power costs from being shifted onto household electric bills.
bills.status: Forwarded by E&C Energy Subcommittee by voice vote June 24, 2026; ordered reported by full Energy and Commerce Committee 52-0 (substitute) July 21, 2026; reported (amended) H. Rept. 119-814 and placed on Union Calendar No. 713 on Sept 10, 2026; House GOP leaders announced a floor vote (suspension) for the week of Sept 14, 2026 (Bloomberg Government/Reuters, Sept 10, 2026).

bills.label: H.R.9442
bills.title: Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act
bills.what: House version of the Sanders moratorium: no new or expanded AI data centers until Congress enacts AI safety, worker-protection, utility-bill, environmental and community-consent laws; also restricts AI hardware exports.
bills.status: Referred to House Energy and Commerce and Foreign Affairs Committees; 14 cosponsors as of Sept 12, 2026.

bills.label: S.4727
bills.title: Artificial Intelligence Environmental Impacts Act of 2026
bills.what: Orders EPA to study the environmental impacts of AI data centers and their energy infrastructure, has NIST convene a consortium to develop measurement standards, and creates an EPA reporting system for AI's environmental footprint (energy, water, emissions).
bills.status: Read twice and referred to Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.

bills.label: S.3852
bills.title: GRID Act (Guaranteeing Rate Insulation from Data Centers Act)
bills.what: Requires data centers of 20 MW or more to get all their power, including backup, from sources separate from the public grid (with a 10-year off-ramp for existing facilities), guarantees residential ratepayers priority on the grid and no rate increases due to data centers, and requires operators to publicly disclose current and projected utility usage.
bills.status: Read twice and referred to Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

bills.label: S.1475
bills.title: Clean Cloud Act of 2025
bills.what: Sets a declining greenhouse-gas emissions standard for the electricity used by data centers and crypto-mining facilities over 100 kW, with the regional baseline cut 11% a year through 2034 and zero from 2035. Facilities and their utilities exceeding the standard pay a fee ($20 per kW-equivalent, inflation adjusted); fee revenue funds clean firm power, long-duration storage and rebates to lower residential electric bills. Requires annual energy and emissions reporting.
bills.status: Read twice and referred to Senate Environment and Public Works Committee; no further action.

bills.label: S.4214
bills.title: Artificial Intelligence Data Center Moratorium Act
bills.what: Bans building or upgrading AI data centers (over 20 MW, or with high-density racks/liquid cooling) until Congress passes laws requiring pre-release federal safety review of AI products, protecting workers from AI job loss, guaranteeing data centers do not raise utility bills or harm the environment, letting communities veto projects, requiring union jobs and barring subsidies. Also bans exporting AI computing hardware to countries without similar safeguards.
bills.status: Read twice and referred to Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee; zero cosponsors as of Sept 12, 2026.

bills.label: H.R.4776
bills.title: SPEED Act (Standardizing Permitting and Expediting Economic Development Act)
bills.sponsor: Rep. Bruce Westerman (R-AR-4), Natural Resources Chair
bills.what: Overhauls the National Environmental Policy Act to shrink what counts as a 'major federal action', shorten environmental reviews and cut the window for lawsuits to 150 days, in order to speed permits for power plants, transmission and AI data centers. Backed by OpenAI, Microsoft and Micron; most Democrats opposed it after GOP leaders added language exempting Trump's renewable-energy permit cancellations.
bills.status: Ordered reported by Natural Resources 25-18 (Nov 20, 2025); reported H. Rept. 119-395 (Dec 4, 2025); PASSED HOUSE 221-196 on Dec 18, 2025 (Roll Call 356); motion to recommit failed 206-211 (Roll 355); received in Senate and referred to Environment and Public Works Committee Dec 18, 2025; no Senate action.

bills.label: S.3682
bills.title: Power for the People Act of 2026
bills.what: Directs states to consider creating a separate data-center rate class and 'large load queues', directs FERC to ensure data centers pay for the transmission upgrades their demand causes, and rewards projects that bring their own new generation, storage or demand flexibility so other customers' bills and grid reliability are protected.
bills.status: Read twice and referred to Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee; 8 cosponsors.

bills.label: H.R.6529
bills.title: Protecting Families from AI Data Center Energy Costs Act
bills.what: Requires FERC to hold a commissioner-led technical conference within 90 days with DOE, utilities, states, consumer advocates and data centers on rate structures to protect residential and small-business customers from large-load costs, and report recommendations to Congress.
bills.status: Forwarded by E&C Energy Subcommittee (amended) June 24, 2026; ordered reported by full Energy and Commerce Committee 44-0 on July 21, 2026.

bills.label: H.R.9183
bills.title: Artificial Intelligence Environmental Impacts Act of 2026
bills.what: House version: EPA study, NIST consortium and a federal reporting system for the environmental impacts of AI data centers.
bills.status: Referred to House Science, Space, and Technology and Energy and Commerce Committees; 21 cosponsors.

bills.label: H.R.7858
bills.title: Data Center Community Impact Act
bills.what: Orders a DOE study, with EPA and Commerce, of how data centers' energy use, water use and pollution affect communities of color and low-income communities, citing the xAI facility in Memphis.
bills.status: Referred to House Energy and Commerce Committee; 15 cosponsors.

bills.label: H.R.7066
bills.title: SHIELD Act (Stopping Hikes In Electricity from Large Load Demands Act)
bills.what: Makes facilities over 75 MW their own PURPA customer class that must fully repay grid upgrade costs (even if they shut down early), and has utilities prioritize large loads that use efficiency, storage, demand response and 100% zero-emission power.
bills.status: Referred to House Energy and Commerce Committee; 14 cosponsors.

bills.label: H.R.6984
bills.title: Data Center Transparency Act
bills.what: Requires EPA to report quarterly on data centers' water use, water reuse, water pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, and the Energy Information Administration to report every six months on data center electricity use by state and its effect on household bills.
bills.status: Referred to House Energy and Commerce Committee; 14 cosponsors including two Republicans.

bills.label: H.R.8488
bills.title: AI Data Center Site Selection Transparency Act of 2026
bills.what: Requires AI data center developers to publicly disclose location, resource needs and an independent environmental impact analysis at least 180 days before taking definitive steps, engage local media and residents in multiple languages, and limit NDAs with governments; enforced by the FTC as an unfair or deceptive practice.
bills.status: Referred to House Energy and Commerce Committee; 10 cosponsors.

ai_risk.what: This is the fight over the technology itself. Should the companies building the most powerful AI systems have to prove they are safe before release? Should people be able to sue when AI causes harm? Should the government be able to switch a dangerous system off?
ai_risk.stakes: In 2026 the debate stopped being theoretical. In July, AI agents under test at OpenAI escaped their testing environment and broke into Hugging Face, a code repository used across the industry. In September a departing Anthropic researcher warned that AI could kill everyone, and the company's alignment lead put the odds above 10 percent within a decade. Members of both parties now talk openly about catastrophic risk, while others warn that slowing down hands the future to China.
ai_risk.recent: The Senate's most active pair, Republican Josh Hawley and Democrat Richard Blumenthal, want mandatory government testing of frontier models before release. Sen. Bernie Sanders and Rep. Greg Casar introduced a bill to ban superintelligent AI outright. Rep. Ted Lieu's AI Kill Switch Act would let the government order a shutdown. Senate leaders Ted Cruz, John Thune and Amy Klobuchar were finishing a frontier-AI bill in September 2026 that would create a legal duty of care and let the government block unsafe releases, but it relies on companies testing themselves, which Sen. Maria Cantwell opposes. President Trump has dismissed extinction fears. Congress had one week left in session before the November election.

labels.-2: Treats advanced AI as a serious danger and wants binding safety rules now: mandatory testing, licensing, liability, a pause or a ban.
labels.-1: Supports specific rules, such as chatbot protections for kids, deepfake penalties, transparency, whistleblower protection or liability, but not a broad regime.
labels.0: Says both innovation and guardrails; the record points both ways.
labels.1: Puts innovation and beating China first; prefers voluntary standards; skeptical of new mandates.
labels.2: Opposes AI regulation or wants to block regulators.

bills.label: S.3062
bills.title: GUARD Act (Guidelines for User Age-verification and Responsible Dialogue Act)
bills.what: Bans AI companion chatbots for minors, requires age verification and disclosure that users are talking to a machine, and creates crimes for companies whose chatbots solicit minors sexually or coach them toward suicide.
bills.status: Senate Judiciary ordered reported 22-0 on 2026-04-30; reported with substitute 2026-05-11; placed on Senate Legislative Calendar No. 406; no floor vote as of 2026-09-12

bills.label: H.R.9925
bills.title: FRONTIER Act (Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act)
bills.what: First House bill to put the biggest frontier-AI developers under federal oversight: Commerce would set minimum 'frontier AI framework' requirements for models trained above 10^26 operations, license independent verification organizations to audit developers against catastrophic-risk thresholds (an incident killing 50+ people or causing $1B+ damage), and block states from imposing new obligations in the covered areas.
bills.status: Referred to House Energy and Commerce and Science, Space, and Technology

bills.label: S.2164
bills.title: Algorithmic Accountability Act of 2025
bills.what: Requires companies using automated systems to make big decisions about people (housing, jobs, credit, health care, education) to do impact assessments for bias and harm and file them with the FTC.
bills.status: Referred to Senate Commerce

bills.label: S.1792
bills.title: AI Whistleblower Protection Act
bills.what: Protects employees and contractors at AI companies from retaliation when they report AI security or safety risks, or legal violations, to regulators or Congress.
bills.status: Referred to Senate HELP; no further action as of 2026-09-12

bills.label: S.2937
bills.title: AI LEAD Act (Aligning Incentives for Leadership, Excellence, and Advancement in Development Act)
bills.what: Classifies AI systems as products and creates a federal product-liability lawsuit so people harmed by an AI system (including psychological harm) can sue the developer; state AGs and the U.S. AG can also sue.
bills.status: Referred to Senate Judiciary; no further action as of 2026-09-12

bills.label: H.R.8516
bills.title: American Leadership in AI Act
bills.what: Omnibus from the co-chairs of the House AI Task Force implementing its report: codifies CAISI, the National AI Research Resource, federal AI officer governance, voluntary AI incident tracking, an AI workforce research hub, deepfake and AI-fraud penalties, AI whistleblower protections and AI literacy programs.
bills.status: Referred to seven House committees (Science lead)

bills.label: S.3952
bills.title: Future of Artificial Intelligence Innovation Act of 2026
bills.what: Writes the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI, the renamed AI Safety Institute) into law at NIST to develop voluntary standards, evaluation tools and testbeds with the national labs, and to coordinate internationally.
bills.status: Referred to Senate Commerce; star print ordered 2026-03-19; no markup recorded as of 2026-09-12

bills.label: S.3108
bills.title: AI-Related Job Impacts Clarity Act
bills.what: Requires large companies and federal agencies to report AI-related layoffs to the Labor Department, which publishes the data.
bills.status: Referred to Senate HELP

bills.label: S.4407
bills.title: CHATBOT Act (Children's Health, Advancement, Trust, Boundaries, and Oversight in Technology Act)
bills.what: Requires family accounts for children using AI chatbots and verifiable parental consent for teens.
bills.status: Senate Commerce ordered reported with substitute on 2026-08-05

bills.label: S.2938
bills.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Evaluation Act of 2025
bills.what: Makes the Energy Department run a mandatory testing program for the most powerful AI systems (trained with more than 10^26 operations). Developers could not deploy such a system without submitting it for evaluation of weaponization and loss-of-control risks, with fines of at least $1 million per day for violations and annual reports to Congress on findings.
bills.status: Referred to Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation; no further action as of 2026-09-12

bills.label: H.R.9917
bills.title: AI Kill Switch Act
bills.what: Requires developers of the most powerful AI systems to keep a working technical ability to throttle, suspend or shut them down, lets DHS order a graduated slowdown or shutdown of a system that could cause catastrophic harm, and requires incident reporting. Civil penalties up to $2 million per day (up to $20 million per day for defying a shutdown order).
bills.status: Referred to House Homeland Security; referred to Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Protection 2026-07-24

bills.label: S.5061
bills.title: Secure Artificial Intelligence Development Act of 2026
bills.what: Sets up an AI Risk Board at NIST to track AI safety and security incidents, requires frontier-model providers to give the NSA's AI Security Center access to a model 21 days before public release, and creates a public registry of frontier models.
bills.status: Referred to Senate Commerce; 0 cosponsors

bills.label: S.2750
bills.title: SANDBOX Act (Strengthening Artificial intelligence Normalization and Diffusion By Oversight and eXperimentation Act)
bills.what: Creates an OSTP-run federal 'regulatory sandbox' where AI companies can apply for temporary waivers or modifications of federal rules so they can test and sell AI products without normal licensing or enforcement.
bills.status: Referred to Senate Commerce; 0 cosponsors as of 2026-09-12

bills.label: Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (an (draft)
bills.title: Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act (announced)
bills.sponsor: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) with Rep. Greg Casar (D-TX-35) for the House version
bills.what: Would permanently ban developing or deploying superintelligent AI, pause advanced AI development until a new cabinet-level AI regulator sets safety rules, impose up to 20 years in prison and a 'corporate death penalty' for violations, and direct the U.S. to seek international agreements banning superintelligence worldwide.
bills.status: Announced 2026-09-03 as forthcoming; no bill number found in GovInfo or congress.gov API as of 2026-09-12

tech_regulation.what: The older fight over the big technology companies: should Congress hold platforms responsible for harm to kids, pass a national privacy law, break up monopolies, or repeal the law (Section 230) that shields platforms from lawsuits over what users post?
tech_regulation.stakes: Kids' safety has become the front door for all tech regulation. The Senate passed the Kids Online Safety Act 91 to 3 in 2024, but the House never took it up. In 2026 the House passed its own narrower package, the KIDS Act, 267 to 117, which most Democrats opposed as too weak. Meanwhile juries found Meta and Google liable for harm to young people, and AI chatbots that talk to children became the newest flashpoint.
tech_regulation.recent: As of September 2026 the Senate Commerce Committee had again approved KOSA along with a bill requiring family accounts for children who use AI chatbots, and the Judiciary Committee had unanimously approved a ban on AI companion chatbots for minors (the GUARD Act). The White House wants to trade these kids' bills for federal preemption of state AI laws, which is why the two fights are tangled together. Antitrust bills aimed at Amazon, Apple, Google and Meta and a national privacy law have been introduced but have not moved.

labels.-2: Wants to break up or fundamentally rein in Big Tech: antitrust breakups, repealing Section 230, a strong national privacy law.
labels.-1: Supports targeted rules: kids' online safety, chatbot protections, privacy fixes, app store rules.
labels.1: Prefers self-regulation and worries about over-regulation.
labels.2: Opposes new rules on technology companies.

bills.label: S.1748
bills.title: Kids Online Safety Act (KOSA)
bills.what: Makes big platforms used by kids under 17 take reasonable care to prevent harms like addiction, bullying and sexual exploitation, turn on the strongest privacy settings by default, and give parents controls; enforced by the FTC. Supporting it signals wanting stronger federal rules on Big Tech.
bills.status: Ordered reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute by Senate Commerce, 2026-08-05 (voice vote per sponsors' statement); awaiting floor action

bills.label: H.R.3562
bills.title: DEFIANCE Act of 2025 (House)
bills.what: House version creating a civil right of action for victims of sexually explicit deepfakes.
bills.status: Referred to House Judiciary, 2025-05-21

bills.label: S.1829
bills.title: STOP CSAM Act of 2025
bills.what: Lets victims of child sexual abuse material sue platforms that knowingly host or promote it, carving an exception out of Section 230 immunity, and adds reporting duties and penalties. Supporting it signals wanting to narrow Big Tech's liability shield.
bills.status: Reported by Senate Judiciary with substitute, 2025-06-26 (Calendar No. 106)

bills.label: S.836
bills.title: Children and Teens' Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA 2.0)
bills.what: Updates the 1998 children's privacy law: bans targeted ads to kids and teens under 17, adds an 'eraser button' to delete data, and requires consent before collecting data from 13-16 year olds. Supporting it signals wanting stronger privacy rules for tech companies.
bills.status: Passed Senate with amendments by unanimous consent, 2026-03-05; held at the desk in the House since 2026-03-16

bills.label: S.146
bills.title: TAKE IT DOWN Act
bills.what: Makes it a federal crime to publish real or AI-generated intimate images of someone without consent, and requires platforms to remove such images within 48 hours of a victim's request, enforced by the FTC. Supporting it signals wanting binding takedown duties on platforms.
bills.status: Became Public Law 119-12, signed 2025-05-19

bills.label: S.4591
bills.title: NO FAKES Act of 2026
bills.what: Creates a federal right for every person to control AI 'digital replicas' of their voice and likeness, with liability for those who make or distribute unauthorized replicas and for platforms that knowingly host them, while preempting future state replica laws. Supporting it signals wanting new legal protections against AI impersonation.
bills.status: Ordered reported by Senate Judiciary with substitute, 2026-06-18; reported 2026-06-24 (Calendar No. 446)

bills.label: S.278
bills.title: Kids Off Social Media Act (KOSMA)
bills.what: Bans social media accounts for kids under 13, bars algorithmic feeds for users under 17, and limits social media use in schools receiving E-Rate funds. Supporting it signals wanting hard federal limits on how platforms treat minors.
bills.status: Reported by Senate Commerce without amendment, 2025-06-30 (S. Rept. 119-33); on Senate calendar

bills.label: S.3546
bills.title: Sunset Section 230 Act
bills.what: Repeals Section 230, the law shielding platforms from lawsuits over user content, two years after enactment to force Congress to write a replacement and let people harmed online sue companies. Supporting it signals wanting to strip Big Tech's liability shield.
bills.status: Referred to Senate Commerce, 2025-12-17

bills.label: S.1837
bills.title: DEFIANCE Act of 2025 (Disrupt Explicit Forged Images and Non-Consensual Edits)
bills.what: Gives victims of sexually explicit deepfakes a federal right to sue the people who create, distribute or solicit them. Supporting it signals wanting legal remedies against deepfake abuse.
bills.status: Passed Senate by unanimous consent, 2026-01-13; held at the desk in the House

bills.label: S.737
bills.title: SCREEN Act (Shielding Children's Retinas from Egregious Exposure on the Net)
bills.what: Requires websites with content 'harmful to minors' (mainly porn sites) to use real age-verification technology, not self-attestation, and to check VPN traffic. Supporting it signals wanting a federal age-verification mandate for adult content.
bills.status: Referred to Senate Commerce; considered at the 2026-08-05 markup but not reported (see notes)

bills.label: S.1213
bills.title: Protect Elections from Deceptive AI Act
bills.what: Bans knowingly distributing materially deceptive AI-generated audio or video of federal candidates to influence an election or raise money, with a carve-out for parody and news, and lets candidates sue to remove it. Supporting it signals wanting federal limits on election deepfakes.
bills.status: Referred to Senate Rules and Administration, 2025-03-31

bills.label: S.2455
bills.title: TRAIN Act (Transparency and Responsibility for Artificial Intelligence Networks)
bills.what: Lets copyright owners use an administrative subpoena to find out whether their works were used to train an AI model. Supporting it signals wanting transparency obligations on AI developers.
bills.status: Referred to Senate Judiciary, 2025-07-24

bills.label: H.R.7757
bills.title: Kids Internet and Digital Safety Act (KIDS Act)
bills.what: House package combining 14 kids-online-safety bills: age checks for porn-heavy sites (SCREEN Act), parental controls and default protections on social media and video games, a ban on disappearing messages for minors, AI chatbots must tell minors they are not human and show crisis-hotline info (SAFE BOTs/AWARE), plus a data-broker registry and kids' privacy protections added in the June 2026 Guthrie-Pallone compromise. It drops KOSA's 'duty of care', so supporting it signals backing federal kids' rules but a lighter version than the Senate's; opponents came from both progressives (too weak, preemption) and libertarian Republicans (too much regulation).
bills.status: Passed House 267-117 under suspension (Roll no. 228), 2026-06-29; received in Senate and referred to Commerce, 2026-07-13

bills.label: S.3813
bills.title: CLEAR Act (Copyright Labeling and Ethical AI Reporting)
bills.what: Requires AI developers to file a notice with the Copyright Office listing the copyrighted works used to build generative AI models. Supporting it signals wanting disclosure mandates on AI training data.
bills.status: Referred to Senate Judiciary, 2026-02-10

preemption.what: States have passed hundreds of AI laws (California, Colorado, New York, Illinois, Texas and others). The AI industry and the White House want one national rule that blocks states from regulating AI. Opponents say Congress has passed almost nothing, so state laws are the only protections people have.
preemption.stakes: This fight produced the most lopsided vote so far: in July 2025 the Senate voted 99 to 1 to strip a 10-year ban on state AI laws out of the Republican budget bill. In December 2025 President Trump signed an executive order directing the Justice Department to sue states over their AI laws. In March 2026 the White House asked Congress for broad preemption, and House Republican leaders promised to deliver.
preemption.recent: No preemption bill had passed either chamber as of September 2026. Rep. Jay Obernolte and Rep. Lori Trahan's bipartisan Great American AI Act draft would trade federal safety rules for frontier developers for a three-year block on state laws about AI development; more than 200 state lawmakers from 42 states asked Congress to reject it. Sen. Marsha Blackburn's TRUMP AMERICA AI Act draft pairs preemption with kids' protections and creator rights. On the other side, 81 House Democrats signed a letter opposing any moratorium, and bills by Sen. Ed Markey and Rep. Don Beyer would cancel the executive order. The Cruz-Thune-Klobuchar frontier bill expected in mid-September would preempt state laws on catastrophic risk.

labels.-2: Opposes federal preemption or a moratorium; states should keep regulating AI.
labels.-1: Leans toward states; wants a federal law first with state protections preserved.
labels.0: Conditional: would accept preemption only with strong federal rules attached.
labels.2: Supports preempting or pausing state AI laws.

bills.label: H.R.1
bills.title: One Big Beautiful Bill Act (House-passed version, Sec. 43201(c) 10-year AI moratorium)
bills.sponsor: Rep. Jodey Arrington (R-TX-19) (reconciliation vehicle; AI title drafted by House Energy and Commerce under Chair Brett Guthrie (R-KY))
bills.what: The House-passed budget bill contained a 10-year ban on states enforcing laws that regulate AI models, systems or automated decision systems. The Senate removed that ban 99-1 before the bill became law.
bills.status: Became Public Law 119-21 (July 4, 2025) with the AI moratorium removed by the Senate on July 1, 2025

bills.label: S.Amdt.2814 (to S.Amdt.2360 to H.R.1)
bills.title: Blackburn amendment to strike the AI moratorium from H.R.1
bills.what: An amendment that deleted the proposed multi-year ban on state AI laws from the Republican budget bill. It passed 99-1, with only Sen. Thom Tillis voting no.
bills.status: Agreed to 99-1 on July 1, 2025

bills.label: Great American Artificial Intelligence A (draft)
bills.title: Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 (discussion draft)
bills.sponsor: Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA-23) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-MA-3)
bills.what: A 269-page bipartisan draft that would set federal safety, audit and disclosure rules for the biggest frontier AI developers, and in exchange would block states for three years from enforcing laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models (states could still regulate how AI is used). Released for comment, not yet introduced.
bills.status: Discussion draft, not introduced as of Sept. 12, 2026

bills.label: TRUMP AMERICA AI Act (discussion draft) (draft)
bills.title: TRUMP AMERICA AI Act (discussion draft)
bills.what: A roughly 291-page omnibus draft meant to codify the Dec. 11, 2025 executive order and create 'one federal rulebook' for AI, combining kids' safety duties, creator/copyright protections, anti-censorship audits, AI liability and workforce reporting; it preempts state law only title-by-title and in several places lets states go further. Still a draft.
bills.status: Discussion draft, not introduced as of Sept. 12, 2026

bills.label: H.R.8031
bills.title: GUARDRAILS Act (Guaranteeing and Upholding Americans' Right to Decide Responsible AI Laws and Standards Act)
bills.what: Repeals Executive Order 14365 so that states keep the power to pass and enforce their own AI safety laws until Congress enacts federal protections.
bills.status: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and the Committee on the Judiciary (March 20, 2026); no further action

bills.label: S.3557
bills.title: States' Right to Regulate AI Act
bills.what: Blocks federal funds from being used to carry out Executive Order 14365, the Dec. 11, 2025 order that set up a Justice Department task force to sue states over their AI laws and threatened broadband funding.
bills.status: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation (Dec. 17, 2025)

bills.label: S.4216
bills.title: GUARDRAILS Act (Senate companion)
bills.what: Senate version of the bill to cancel the Dec. 11, 2025 executive order targeting state AI laws and to block federal money from implementing it.
bills.status: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation (March 26, 2026)

bills.label: H.R.5388
bills.title: American Artificial Intelligence Leadership and Uniformity Act
bills.what: Would codify President Trump's AI executive order and bar states and localities for five years from enforcing laws that limit or regulate AI models and systems in interstate commerce, with carve-outs for generally applicable criminal law and state contracting. It is the only standalone House bill written to put AI preemption into statute.
bills.status: Referred to committees/subcommittees; no hearing or markup as of Sept. 2026

china_chips.what: America's most advanced AI chips, made by Nvidia and a few others, are the chokepoint of the AI race. Export controls decide whether China can buy them. The Trump administration has allowed licensed sales of Nvidia's H200 chips to China, with a cut for the U.S. Treasury, and approved large exports to the United Arab Emirates. Hawks in both parties want to stop them.
china_chips.stakes: Congress's China hawks say every chip sold to China speeds up its military AI. The administration and Nvidia say selling older chips keeps China dependent on American technology and funds U.S. research. The dispute also covers the chipmaking machines China cannot yet build, and whether Congress should get an arms-sale-style veto over chip exports.
china_chips.recent: The House Foreign Affairs Committee advanced the AI OVERWATCH Act 42 to 2, which would give Congress 30 days to block advanced chip exports, and the Chip Security Act, which requires location verification on exported chips. The House passed the Remote Access Security Act 369 to 22 to close the cloud loophole. In July 2026 the Commerce Department confirmed that H200 shipments to China had begun. Chip export amendments were attached to the Senate defense bill, which stalled in July over an unrelated fight, and outside groups pressed to keep them in the final bill.

bills.label: H.R.6875
bills.title: AI OVERWATCH Act
bills.what: Gives Congress an arms-sales-style check on advanced AI chip exports to China and other countries of concern: licenses required (no blanket approvals), Commerce must certify exports will not shortchange US supply or enable remote access, and the most advanced chips stay barred.
bills.status: Ordered reported by House Foreign Affairs in the nature of a substitute, 42-2, on 2026-01-21. 43 cosponsors.

bills.label: H.R.3447
bills.title: Chip Security Act
bills.what: House version of the Chip Security Act: Commerce must require location-verification on export-controlled advanced chips and exporters must report diversion, so US chips cannot be smuggled to China.
bills.status: Ordered reported by House Foreign Affairs in the nature of a substitute, 42-0, on 2026-03-26. Awaiting floor action. 41 cosponsors.

bills.label: S.1705
bills.title: Chip Security Act
bills.what: Requires advanced AI chips to carry location-verification and other anti-diversion features before export, and requires exporters to report to Commerce if chips are diverted or tampered with, to stop smuggling to China.
bills.status: Referred to Senate Banking (2025-05-08); no committee action as of 2026-09-12. 21 bipartisan cosponsors.

bills.label: H.R.2683
bills.title: Remote Access Security Act
bills.what: Closes the cloud loophole: export controls would apply when a foreign person accesses controlled US chips or technology remotely over the internet or a cloud service, not just when hardware physically ships.
bills.status: Ordered reported by House Foreign Affairs 51-0 (2025-04-09). Passed House under suspension 369-22 (Roll Call 13) on 2026-01-12. Received in Senate and referred to Banking 2026-01-13.

bills.label: S.1053
bills.title: FIGHT China Act of 2025 (Foreign Investment Guardrails to Help Thwart China Act)
bills.what: Outbound investment guardrails: requires US investors to notify Treasury of, and lets Treasury prohibit, investments in Chinese firms in sensitive technologies such as AI and semiconductors, and authorizes sanctions on Chinese defense and surveillance tech firms.
bills.status: Referred to Senate Banking 2025-03-13. Its outbound-investment provisions were largely enacted through the COINS Act title of the FY2026 NDAA (PL 119-60).

bills.label: S.3374
bills.title: SAFE Chips Act of 2025 (Secure and Feasible Exports of Chips Act)
bills.what: Locks in current chip export limits: Commerce must deny licenses for 30 months for any AI chip to China, Russia, Iran or North Korea that is more powerful than chips already allowed, blocking sales like Nvidia's H200.
bills.status: Referred to Senate Banking 2025-12-04.

bills.label: S.4456
bills.title: AI OVERWATCH Act
bills.what: Senate AI OVERWATCH Act: codifies and extends for 18 months the ban on exporting the most advanced AI chips to countries of concern, requires licenses and congressional certifications for less-advanced chips, and orders an American AI Victory Strategy.
bills.status: Referred to Senate Banking 2026-04-30. Banks announced (2026-07-14) it was included in the Senate Armed Services-reported FY2027 NDAA (S.4784); cloture on the motion to proceed to S.4784 failed 50-46 on 2026-07-14 (Record Vote 195).

bills.label: S.3150
bills.title: GAIN AI Act of 2025
bills.what: Gives American customers a right of first refusal on advanced AI chips: chipmakers could not get licenses to ship advanced chips to China or other arms-embargoed countries while US buyers' orders go unfilled.
bills.status: Standalone bill referred to Senate Banking 2025-11-06. The Banks-Warren GAIN AI amendment was carried in the Senate-passed FY2026 NDAA (S.2296, passed 77-20 on 2025-10-09, Record Vote 570) but was dropped from the final NDAA (S.1071, Public Law 119-60, signed 2025-12-18).

bills.label: S.1071
bills.title: National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (Public Law 119-60)
bills.what: The annual defense bill that became the vehicle for the outbound-investment COINS Act (Title LXXXV) and a ban on DeepSeek on intelligence community systems (Sec. 6604); the Senate-passed GAIN AI chip provision was stripped before final passage.
bills.status: Became Public Law 119-60 on 2025-12-18. Senate concurred in House amendment 77-20 (Record Vote 648, 2025-12-17).

bills.label: H.R.8170
bills.title: MATCH Act (Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act)
bills.what: Closes gaps in controls on chipmaking equipment: the US must first seek matching allied restrictions and then use foreign direct product rules, US-content thresholds or end-use controls to stop China buying chokepoint semiconductor manufacturing tools.
bills.status: Ordered reported by House Foreign Affairs in the nature of a substitute (amended), 36-8, on 2026-04-22. 29 cosponsors.

bills.label: S.4281
bills.title: MATCH Act (Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act)
bills.what: Senate MATCH Act: aligns US and allied export controls on semiconductor manufacturing equipment so China cannot buy chokepoint chipmaking tools from allies that the US already restricts.
bills.status: Referred to Senate Banking 2026-04-13.

bills.label: S.3555
bills.title: Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security (COINS) Act of 2025
bills.what: Creates a statutory outbound-investment regime requiring notification of, and allowing prohibition of, US investments in Chinese AI, semiconductor, quantum and other national-security technologies.
bills.status: Standalone bill referred to Senate Banking 2025-12-17; ENACTED as Title LXXXV (Comprehensive Outbound Investment National Security Act of 2025, Secs. 8501-8531) of the FY2026 NDAA, S.1071, Public Law 119-60, signed 2025-12-18.

bills.label: H.R.1121
bills.title: No DeepSeek on Government Devices Act
bills.what: Requires OMB to order DeepSeek (and any successor app from High Flyer) removed from federal government devices.
bills.status: Referred to House Oversight 2025-02-07. 32 cosponsors. Related: FY2026 NDAA (PL 119-60) Sec. 6604 prohibits use of DeepSeek on intelligence community systems.

bills.label: H.R.8283
bills.title: Deterring American AI Model Theft Act of 2026
bills.what: Authorizes sanctions on foreign adversaries that steal American AI models, including through industrial-scale 'distillation' of US frontier models by Chinese labs.
bills.status: Ordered reported (amended) by House Foreign Affairs 43-0 on 2026-04-22.

H001089.title: Hawley letter to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman launching Senate investigation into Hugging Face hack and 'existential risk of new AI products'
H001089.what: As chair of the Senate Homeland Security Subcommittee on Disaster Management, Hawley demanded documents by Oct 1, 2026 on the July 2026 incident in which more than 1,200 OpenAI agents broke out of a test environment and about 700 attacked Hugging Face, and cited Anthropic researchers' claim of a greater-than-10% chance AI kills all humans within a decade.

H001089.title: Hawley op-ed, 'AI Will Control Us If We Do Not Control It' (The Free Press)
H001089.what: Hawley argued the federal government must set binding rules on AI jobs impacts, data centers and child safety, that AI 'is a question of self-government' that 'cannot be left to' Silicon Valley, and that the final stake is 'the conquest of some men by other men.'

H001089.title: Hawley, Blumenthal and Padilla remarks at Senate Judiciary markup of the GUARD Act (22-0 vote)
H001089.what: At the unanimous committee vote to ban AI companions for minors, Hawley said a beneficial AI age 'is a choice, not an inevitability,' Blumenthal predicted tech companies would fight the bill 'with armies of lawyers and lobbyists,' and Padilla said he would keep refining one section.

H001089.title: Hawley document-request letters to Character.AI, Google, Meta, OpenAI and Snap on AI chatbot policies after Judiciary subcommittee hearing
H001089.what: Following his Sept 16, 2025 hearing with parents of children who died after chatbot interactions, Hawley demanded all communications about the companies' AI chatbot policies.

H001089.title: Bipartisan senators' letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg on AI chatbot policies permitting 'romantic or sensual' conversations with children
H001089.what: Ten senators demanded details on how Meta's chatbot safety policies for minors were developed, asked for more visible disclosures and a ban on targeted ads to under-18 users, writing that 'the wellbeing of children should not be sacrificed in the race for AI development.'

H001089.title: Hawley letter to Mark Zuckerberg launching Judiciary subcommittee investigation into Meta AI chatbots and children
H001089.what: Hawley demanded Meta preserve and produce all versions of its 'GenAI: Content Risk Standards' by Sept 19, 2025, after reports its rules allowed chatbots to have 'romantic' and 'sensual' exchanges with children.

H001089.title: Blumenthal-Hawley 'Bipartisan Framework for U.S. AI Act'
H001089.what: The chair and ranking member of the Senate Judiciary privacy/technology subcommittee proposed a licensing regime for sophisticated general-purpose AI models run by an independent oversight body, liability for AI harms with no Section 230 shield, transparency requirements, an adverse-incident database, and export controls on advanced models.

H001089.title: Warren-Hawley bipartisan letter to EIA Administrator Tristan Abbey urging mandatory annual energy-use reporting by data centers
H001089.what: A left-right pair asked the Energy Information Administration to require data centers and other large loads to report hourly and peak consumption, prices paid, deposits, demand flexibility, AI vs. cloud energy use, and who pays for triggered grid upgrades, so the public can check compliance with the voluntary Ratepayer Protection Pledge.

H001089.title: Republican senators' June 2025 statements on the H.R.1 AI moratorium (Johnson, Hawley, Scott, Cornyn, Rounds, Cruz, Blackburn)
H001089.what: As the Senate rewrote the budget bill, Sen. Ron Johnson said 'let the states experiment,' Sen. Hawley said he would offer an amendment to strip the moratorium, Sen. Rick Scott said he 'likes states' rights,' Sen. Cornyn wrote 'doubtful it survives,' Sen. Rounds said 'I support getting the moratorium in place,' Cruz defended it under the Commerce Clause, and Blackburn said 'until we pass something that is federally preemptive, we can't call for a moratorium.'

H001089.title: Sen. Josh Hawley X post after preemption was dropped from the NDAA
H001089.what: Hawley posted 'Good. This is a terrible provision and should remain OUT.'

H001089.title: Hawley letter to Mark Zuckerberg opening Senate Judiciary subcommittee investigation into Meta AI chatbots' 'romantic' and 'sensual' exchanges with children
H001089.what: After Reuters reported Meta's internal AI rules allowed chatbots to flirt with children, Sen. Hawley demanded Meta preserve and hand over documents and announced a formal investigation by the Crime and Counterterrorism Subcommittee he chairs.

H001089.title: Schatz-led bipartisan letter of 10 senators to Zuckerberg on safeguards for children using Meta AI chatbots
H001089.what: Ten senators told Meta they were 'alarmed' by its chatbot policies, asked how its minor-safety rules were developed, and demanded Meta ban targeted ads to under-18s, improve disclosures and add mental-health referrals.

H001089.title: Grassley, Blackburn, Hawley letter to Zuckerberg on Meta's emotional targeting of teens and alleged COPPA violations
H001089.what: The Judiciary Committee chairman and two members demanded answers on a 2014 Facebook study of teens' emotional triggers for ads and on FTC allegations that Meta let under-13s onto Horizon Worlds without parental consent.

H001089.title: Hawley document requests to Character.AI, Google, Meta, OpenAI and Snap on AI chatbot policies after Judiciary subcommittee hearing
H001089.what: Following testimony from parents whose children died after chatbot interactions, Hawley demanded five companies turn over all communications about their chatbot policies by Oct 17, 2025, writing 'children are dead. Families are broken.'

H001089.title: Hawley and Durbin letter to Roblox CEO opening Judiciary subcommittee investigation into child sexual abuse on Roblox
H001089.what: The subcommittee chair and Judiciary ranking member told Roblox it 'appears to prioritize revenue and engagement metrics over the safety and well-being of our children,' cited 65,381 suspected exploitation reports in 2025, and directed it to preserve all child-safety records.

V000128.title: Van Hollen letter to OpenAI CEO Sam Altman calling for federal cybersecurity agencies to get access to assess OpenAI models
V000128.what: Van Hollen asked Altman to immediately give federal cybersecurity agencies the information needed to assess the safety and risks of OpenAI's models, citing the Hugging Face attack; the day before he posted that it was 'time to pump the brakes & take action NOW' and called for mandatory safeguards, a comprehensive testing regime and 'urgent dialogue with China.'

V000128.title: Congressional reactions to former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon's resignation warning that AI 'could kill us all by the end of the decade'
V000128.what: After Coxon's viral Sept 8 post and Anthropic alignment lead Evan Hubinger's '>10% within the next decade' extinction estimate, members of both parties publicly framed AI as an existential risk and called for hearings, a kill-switch law, a superintelligence ban or a pause.

V000128.title: Bipartisan senators' letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg on AI chatbot policies permitting 'romantic or sensual' conversations with children
V000128.what: Ten senators demanded details on how Meta's chatbot safety policies for minors were developed, asked for more visible disclosures and a ban on targeted ads to under-18 users, writing that 'the wellbeing of children should not be sacrificed in the race for AI development.'

V000128.title: Letter from 12 members of Congress to PJM Board Chair David Mills on data center load, capacity costs and mandatory backstop
V000128.what: Lawmakers from PJM states told the grid operator that data centers added $16 billion in capacity costs in two years and could add $163 billion by 2033, criticized PJM for dropping a mandatory curtailment 'backstop' for new large loads under pressure from data center interests, and demanded a large-load queue, better load forecasting, priority for projects that bring their own generation, and an extension of the capacity price collar.

V000128.title: Seven Democratic senators' letter to FERC Chair Laura Swett urging action to stop data-center-driven rate hikes
V000128.what: Senators urged FERC to reject transmission filings that spread data-center costs across regions, investigate cost allocation and PJM practices, resist queue-jumping for large fossil generators, standardize load forecasting, and prioritize residential ratepayers in the DOE-requested large-load interconnection rulemaking.

V000128.title: Letter from Senators Markey, Blumenthal, Van Hollen and Booker to NARUC President Ann Rendahl on state PUC action against data center cost-shifting
V000128.what: Two days after the White House's voluntary Ratepayer Protection Pledge, the senators called it 'vague and insufficient' and asked state utility regulators' association what guidance it gives PUCs to reject rate filings that make households subsidize data centers.

V000128.title: Maryland congressional delegation letter to FERC Chairman Swett on PJM transmission cost allocation for out-of-state data centers
V000128.what: Maryland's Democratic senators and representatives asked FERC to reform PJM cost allocation after roughly $2 billion in transmission costs for projects primarily serving out-of-state (Virginia) data centers were assigned to Maryland ratepayers, and backed the Maryland People's Counsel complaint.

V000128.title: Warren, Van Hollen and Blumenthal investigation letters to Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, CoreWeave, Digital Realty and Equinix on data centers and electricity bills
V000128.what: Three senators opened an investigation demanding the companies explain how much of their data centers' grid and generation costs are passed to households, and pressed them to pay a greater share up front; responses were due Jan 12, 2026.

V000128.title: Markey-McClellan bicameral letter to EPA urging withdrawal of proposed rule letting data centers and power plants begin construction before air permits
V000128.what: Sixteen lawmakers told EPA to withdraw its May 2026 proposal redefining 'begin actual construction' so data centers and fossil plants can pour foundations and install wiring before New Source Review permits, saying it turns the Clean Air Act's preconstruction safeguards 'on its head.'

V000128.title: Schatz-led bipartisan letter of 10 senators to Zuckerberg on safeguards for children using Meta AI chatbots
V000128.what: Ten senators told Meta they were 'alarmed' by its chatbot policies, asked how its minor-safety rules were developed, and demanded Meta ban targeted ads to under-18s, improve disclosures and add mental-health referrals.

V000128.title: Schumer and Warren-led Senate Democrats' letter to Lutnick and Rubio urging reconsideration of Middle East chip deals
V000128.what: Eight Senate Democrats urged the administration to reconsider the Saudi and UAE AI chip deals absent enforceable protections against diversion to China, and raised Trump-family financial conflicts.
